(Entertainment Weekly) -- It was a glass half-full, glass half-empty kind of weekend at the box office for "Funny People," writer-director Judd Apatow's comedic meditation on fame, humor, life, and death. Adam Sandler and Seth Rogen star in "Funny People," which took the No. 1 slot at the box office this weekend. According to figures from Hollywood.com Box Office, it opened at the top spot with an estimated $23.4 million, better than Apatow's The 40 Year-Old Virgin ($21.4 million) -- hence, the glass is half full. But that figure is far lower than the debut for Apatow's "Knocked Up" ($30.7 million), and it's the worst opening for a comedy for star Adam Sander since his 2000 turkey "Little Nicky" -- hence, the glass is half empty. Of course, "Funny People" was billed more as a thoughtful dramedy than a balls-out Sandler laugh-fest, and when matched against the opening frames for Sandler's serious efforts "Reign Over Me," "Spanglish," and "Punch-Drunk Love," Funny People is far and away the winner -- and the glass is half full again. But whether it's a comedy, drama, or dramedy, "Funny People's" $75 million budget is quite the handful of pretty pennies, and with a shaky "B-" Cinemascore, the film is going to have a hard time overcoming tepid word-of-mouth -- and we're back to the half-empty glass. So let's just move on, shall we? The cup of a certain adolescent wizard, meanwhile, definitely runneth over. Thanks to its debut on IMAX (and the premium ticket prices that come with it), "Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince" came in second with $17.7 million, a soft 40 percent drop from last weekend for $255.5 million total. At this rate, the film is well on its way to the upper ranks of the 'Potter' franchise. The guinea pigs of "G-Force" were right on its heels at third place, nibbling up $17.1 million, a decent 46 percent drop for a two-week cume of $66.5 million. And Katherine Heigl's romcom "The Ugly Truth" took in an additional $13 million, a 53 percent drop for fourth place and $54.5 million total. Of the two other wide releases this weekend, at least the sci-fi family comedy "Aliens in the Attic" -- which grossed a meager $7.8 million for fifth place -- broke into the top 10. The torture porn flick "The Collector" collected a grisly $3.6 million and plopped dead at 11th place. Box office on a whole was down a massive 22 percent from last year, when The "Dark Knight" and "The Mummy: Tomb of the Dragon Emperor" both took in over $40 million, but the specialty market showed some vibrant signs of life. Bone fide indie hit "(500) Days of Summer" expanded to 266 theaters for $2.7 million, a $10,338 per theater average. And three widely disparate films opened in four theaters each to healthy per theater averages: The quirky romantic comedy "Adam" ($16,566 per theater), the stylish vampire film "Thirst" ($13,793 per theater), and the eco-thriller-cum-documentary "The Cove" ($13,600 per theater). Finally, a true milestone was reached this weekend by "The Hangover." With $5.1 million this weekend for a running total of $255.8 million, the summer's biggest die hard blockbuster has passed "Star Trek" and (for a brief moment) "Harry Potter 6" as the third highest grossing movie of the year. (Entertainment Weekly) -- It was a glass-half-full, glass-half-empty weekend at the box office for “Funny People,” writer-director Judd Apatow’s comedic meditation on fame, humor, life, and death. Adam Sandler and Seth Rogen star in the film, which claimed the No. 1 spot this weekend. According to figures from Hollywood.com Box Office, “Funny People” opened with an estimated $23.4 million—surpassing Apatow’s “The 40-Year-Old Virgin” ($21.4 million), hence the glass half full. Yet that total fell well short of the debut for Apatow’s “Knocked Up” ($30.7 million), and marked the weakest comedy opening for star Adam Sandler since his 2000 turkey “Little Nicky”—hence the glass half empty.

Of course, “Funny People” was marketed less as an all-out Sandler laugh-fest than as a thoughtful dramedy, and when measured against the opening weekends of Sandler’s more serious efforts—“Reign Over Me,” “Spanglish,” and “Punch-Drunk Love”—it is far and away the winner. The glass, once again, is half full. But whether classified as a comedy, drama, or dramedy, “Funny People” carries a hefty $75 million budget, and with a shaky “B-” Cinemascore, the film may struggle to overcome tepid word of mouth. And so, we return to the half-empty glass.

So let’s move on, shall we?

The cup of a certain adolescent wizard, meanwhile, most definitely runneth over. Thanks to its debut on IMAX—and the premium ticket prices that come with it—“Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince” came in second with $17.7 million, a modest 40 percent drop from last weekend, bringing its total to $255.5 million. At this pace, the film is well on its way to the upper ranks of the “Potter” franchise.

The guinea pigs of “G-Force” were close behind in third place, nibbling up $17.1 million—a decent 46 percent drop—for a two-week cumulative total of $66.5 million. Katherine Heigl’s romcom “The Ugly Truth” earned an additional $13 million, a 53 percent decline, landing in fourth place with $54.5 million total.

Of the weekend’s two other wide releases, at least the sci-fi family comedy “Aliens in the Attic”—which grossed a modest $7.8 million—managed to break into the top 10, finishing fifth. The torture-porn flick “The Collector” collected a grisly $3.6 million and landed lifelessly in 11th place.

Overall box office was down a steep 22 percent from last year, when “The Dark Knight” and “The Mummy: Tomb of the Dragon Emperor” each took in more than $40 million. Still, the specialty market showed vibrant signs of life. Bona fide indie hit “(500) Days of Summer” expanded to 266 theaters and earned $2.7 million, averaging $10,338 per theater. Meanwhile, three widely disparate films opened in four theaters each to healthy per-theater averages: the quirky romantic comedy “Adam” ($16,566 per theater), the stylish vampire film “Thirst” ($13,793 per theater), and the eco-thriller-cum-documentary “The Cove” ($13,600 per theater).

Finally, “The Hangover” reached a true milestone this weekend. With $5.1 million earned over the frame and a running total of $255.8 million, the summer’s biggest die-hard blockbuster passed “Star Trek” and, for a brief moment, “Harry Potter 6” to become the third-highest-grossing movie of the year.

counterfactuals.output:
## Box Office: “Funny People” Laughs Its Way to No. 1 — Depending on How You Look at It

**Glass half-full:** Adam Sandler and Judd Apatow proved there’s still room at the summer box office for a grown-up, R-rated comedy-drama about mortality, fame, and stand-up punch lines. **“Funny People” debuted in first place with $23.4 million**, giving Universal a weekend win and handing Apatow another opening in the comedy big leagues.

**Glass half-empty:** For a movie starring Sandler — usually one of Hollywood’s most reliable opening-weekend draws — and carrying Apatow’s brand name, **$23.4 million felt more like a polite chuckle than a belly laugh**. The film’s lengthy running time, darker tone, and mixed word-of-mouth suggested this was never going to play like “Knocked Up” or a typical Sandler comedy.

In other words: “Funny People” won the weekend, but it didn’t exactly kill.

The weekend’s runner-up was **“Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince,”** which continued its strong summer run with about **$17.7 million**, pushing the wizard franchise deeper into blockbuster territory. Close behind was Disney’s guinea-pig action comedy **“G-Force,”** which added roughly **$17.1 million** after opening at No. 1 the previous weekend.

The Katherine Heigl-Gerard Butler romantic comedy **“The Ugly Truth”** held reasonably well with about **$13 million**, while the family sci-fi newcomer **“Aliens in the Attic”** opened softly with around **$8 million** — a result that suggests kids may have already had their fill of animated mammoths, secret-agent rodents, and transforming robots.

Horror entry **“Orphan”** followed with about **$7.3 million**, while summer holdovers including **“Ice Age: Dawn of the Dinosaurs,” “The Hangover,” “The Proposal,”** and **“Transformers: Revenge of the Fallen”** continued to pad their totals.

### The “Funny People” split decision

The tricky thing about “Funny People” is that it was sold with familiar ingredients — Sandler, Apatow, Seth Rogen, comedians playing comedians — but delivered something more melancholy than the ads may have promised. That makes the opening weekend easy to spin two ways:

- **Half-full:** A nearly two-and-a-half-hour, R-rated dramedy opened at No. 1 in late summer. That’s not nothing.
- **Half-empty:** With Sandler in front and Apatow behind the camera, expectations were higher than “respectable.”
- **Half-full:** The movie could find legs with adults if word-of-mouth emphasizes its ambition and performances.
- **Half-empty:** Comedies usually need strong audience enthusiasm, and a darker, longer film may face a tougher second weekend.

### Specialty box office: Indies find their own laughs — and audiences

Away from the multiplex crush, specialty releases offered some of the weekend’s more interesting per-screen stories.

Fox Searchlight’s **“(500) Days of Summer”** continued to build momentum as it expanded, drawing strong business from indie-minded audiences and proving that a stylish, bittersweet romantic comedy could thrive as counterprogramming to franchise fare.

The political satire **“In the Loop”** also performed well in limited release, benefiting from sharp reviews and an audience hungry for rapid-fire verbal warfare. Meanwhile, documentaries and smaller art-house titles — including **“The Cove”** and other limited-market releases — found modest but encouraging traction with upscale and specialty crowds.

And that may be the weekend’s real glass-half-full takeaway: while the No. 1 movie inspired debate over whether its opening was a triumph or a warning sign, audiences still showed up for a surprisingly wide menu — raunchy comedy, teen wizards, family adventure, romantic farce, horror, indie romance, and political satire.

Not a bad weekend for Hollywood. Even if some people are arguing over how funny the funny people really were.

## “Funny People” Tops Weekend Box Office, but Laughs Fall Short of Expectations

**August 2009** — Judd Apatow’s *Funny People* claimed the No. 1 spot at the North American box office over the weekend, but its victory came with an asterisk. The Adam Sandler–Seth Rogen dramedy opened in first place with an estimated **$22.7 million**, a respectable debut but below the stronger numbers many industry watchers had expected from a high-profile summer comedy.

Released by Universal in **3,008 theaters**, *Funny People* averaged roughly **$7,500 per location**. The film benefited from the combined drawing power of Sandler, Rogen, and Apatow, whose previous hits included *The 40-Year-Old Virgin* and *Knocked Up*. Still, the film’s lengthy running time, R rating, and more dramatic tone likely limited its broader mainstream appeal.

The opening was especially notable because Sandler’s comedies often debut much higher. While *Funny People* still won the weekend, it did not generate the kind of breakout comedy numbers that Universal may have hoped for during the heart of summer movie season.

### Top Weekend Box Office Rankings

1. **Funny People** — **$22.7 million**  
   The weekend’s top film opened below expectations despite major star power and strong marketing. Its mix of comedy and melancholy drama may have made it a tougher sell than a typical Adam Sandler vehicle.

2. **Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince** — **$17.7 million**  
   Warner Bros.’ wizarding blockbuster remained a major force in its third weekend. The film pushed its domestic total to approximately **$255 million**, continuing one of the summer’s strongest runs.

3. **G-Force** — **$17.1 million**  
   Disney’s 3D family adventure held well after opening at No. 1 the previous weekend. The talking-guinea-pig action comedy lifted its domestic total to around **$66 million**.

4. **The Ugly Truth** — **$13.0 million**  
   The Katherine Heigl–Gerard Butler romantic comedy continued to draw adult audiences, bringing its domestic gross to roughly **$54 million** after two weekends.

5. **Aliens in the Attic** — **$8.0 million**  
   Fox’s family sci-fi comedy debuted modestly in fifth place. The film opened in more than 3,000 theaters but struggled to stand out in a crowded summer marketplace.

6. **Orphan** — **$7.3 million**  
   The horror thriller dipped in its second weekend, raising its domestic total to about **$27 million**.

7. **Ice Age: Dawn of the Dinosaurs** — **$5.3 million**  
   The animated sequel continued to show staying power, bringing its domestic total to approximately **$182 million**.

8. **The Hangover** — **$5.1 million**  
   One of the summer’s biggest surprise hits remained in the top 10 yet again. The Warner Bros. comedy climbed to about **$256 million** domestically.

9. **The Proposal** — **$4.8 million**  
   Sandra Bullock and Ryan Reynolds’ romantic comedy continued its impressive run, nearing **$149 million** in North America.

10. **Transformers: Revenge of the Fallen** — **$4.6 million**  
   Michael Bay’s effects-heavy sequel added to its blockbuster total, reaching roughly **$388 million** domestically.

### A Soft Win for Universal

Although *Funny People* led the weekend, the result was considered somewhat muted given the talent involved. Apatow had become one of the most recognizable comedy brands of the decade, while Sandler remained one of Hollywood’s most reliable box office stars. But unlike a broad, high-concept comedy, *Funny People* was marketed as a more personal, bittersweet story about fame, mortality, and stand-up comedy.

That tone may have helped the film with critics and older viewers, but it also made the movie less accessible to audiences looking for a straightforward summer laugh fest. Its opening suggested that while the Apatow brand was still powerful, it was not immune to the challenges of selling more adult, character-driven material during blockbuster season.

Meanwhile, holdovers such as *Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince*, *G-Force*, *The Ugly Truth*, and *The Hangover* demonstrated the depth of the summer box office. Family films, romantic comedies, franchise sequels, and R-rated comedies all remained competitive as August began.
